common_name: Tanima-no-Yuki Azalea (Snow in the Valley Satsuki Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Tanima-no-Yuki is one of the oldest and most widely distributed Satsuki cultivars, long used as breeding stock for Kaho, Aikoku, and other classic Satsuki lines.

directions: Tanima-no-Yuki, whose Japanese name translates roughly to 'snow in the valley,' is a historic Satsuki azalea prized for its restless, unpredictable flower pattern: white-ground blooms irregularly striped, stippled, and flecked in shades of pink to carmine-red, with the proportion of white to color varying widely from plant to plant and even flower to flower on the same shrub. Because it sports so readily, it has thrown off numerous named color breaks over the decades and remains a workhorse parent in Satsuki breeding programs as well as a popular subject for bonsai, where its late-spring to early-summer bloom and small, glossy leaves suit careful training. Grow it like other Satsuki selections, in humus-rich, acidic, evenly moist soil with light shade through the hottest part of the day, and prune only in the few weeks right after bloom since next year's buds set soon afterward.

common_name: Lakeside Cupcake Hosta (Miniature Cupped Blue-Green Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Lakeside Cupcake is part of the extensive Lakeside breeding series and later threw the white-centered sport Half and Half.

directions: Lakeside Cupcake is a miniature-to-small selection from the Lakeside breeding series, forming a dense, tight mound of rounded, strongly cupped blue-green leaves whose deeply folded shape gives the cultivar its name. Pale lavender flowers rise on short scapes just above the foliage in summer, but the plant is grown primarily for its neat, cup-leaved foliage habit rather than for bloom. Its small scale makes it a good fit for the front of a shaded border, a trough, or a rock garden, where larger hostas would quickly crowd it out. Keep soil consistently moist, since small-leaved hostas like this one have less reserve to draw on during hot, dry spells than larger-leaved cultivars.
